text: Kazakhstan, the largest country fully within the Eurasian Steppe, has served as a historical crossroads and home to numerous peoples, states, and empires. Human activity began with Homo erectus one million to 800,000 years ago in the Karatau Mountains and the Caspian and Balkhash areas, followed by Neanderthals from 140,000 to 40,000 years ago in the Karatau Mountains and central Kazakhstan. Modern Homo sapiens appeared from 40,000 to 12,000 years ago in southern, central, and eastern Kazakhstan. After the end of the last glacial period (12,500 to 5,000 years ago), human settlement spread across the country, leading to the extinction of the mammoth and woolly rhinoceros. Hunter-gatherer groups developed bows and boats and used domesticated wolves and traps for hunting. The Neolithic Revolution brought animal husbandry and agriculture, giving rise to the Atbasar, Kelteminar, Botai, and Ust-Narym cultures. The Botai culture (3600–3100 BC) is credited with the first domestication of horses, and ceramics and polished-stone tools appeared during this period. The fourth and third millennia saw the beginning of metal production, including copper tools and casting molds, while ore mining developed in central Kazakhstan during the second millennium BC. Climate changes caused population shifts; a dry period from the end of the second millennium to the beginning of the first millennium BC led to depopulation of arid belts and river-valley oases, with people moving north to the forest steppe. After the end of this arid period, nomadic populations migrated into Kazakhstan from the west and east, repopulating abandoned areas, including several Indo-Iranians known collectively as the Saka. In the 13th century, the region was part of the Mongol Empire and later controlled by the Golden Horde. After the Horde's decline, it became part of the Uzbek Khanate, whose nomads were known as Uzbeks due to their conversion to Islam under Uzbeg Khan (1313–1341). The Kazakh Khanate emerged from the merging of Mongols and Turkic peoples in the Kipchak Steppe. In the 1450s, Zhanibek Khan and Kerey Khan, two Jochid princes, broke away from the Uzbek Khanate and established the Kazakh Khanate. The Kazakh identity formed when eastern nomads of the Kipchak Steppe split into Kazakhs and Shibanid Uzbeks in the early 16th century. The Kazakhs, like other Chinggisid peoples such as the Shibanid Uzbeks, Crimean Tatars, and Mangyt/Nogais, shared a common Turkic language, Mongol traditions, Chinggisid royal lineage, and Sunni Islam. By the 16th century, the Kazakhs had asserted independence and expanded their territory, transforming their khanate into a nomadic empire, reaching its peak in the 16th century as the last remaining Chinggisid state. During the reign of the three sons of Kasym Khan, khan authority weakened, leading to the fragmentation of the khanate into three hordes: the Great Horde in southeastern Kazakhstan north of the Tien Shan, the Middle Horde in the central steppe near the Aral Sea, and the Little Horde between the Aral Sea and the Ural River. The khan’s power was often constrained by tribal leaders known as sultans and even more so by beys and batyrs, heads of clan-based communities. Although the khans nominally commanded a military, their authority depended on the loyalty of these local leaders. The final son of Kasym Khan, Haqnazar, overcame these challenges, reunited the three hordes, and expanded his power beyond the steppes, bringing under control the Bashkirs, Kyrgyzes, Nogais, and territories such as the Kazan, Siberian, and Astrakhan khanates, as well as cities like Bukhara, Khiva, and Tashkent. According to Rychkov, Haqnazar’s reign was marked by brutal consolidation, including heavy tributes, restrictions on movement and resources, limiting households to one cooking pot per three, confiscating livestock, goods, and children, and prohibiting land ownership and crossing certain rivers, which impoverished neighboring peoples but strengthened his dominion. His successors continued military campaigns, including Tevkkel Khan (1586–1598), who briefly captured Samarkand. By the early 17th century, internal unity eroded, leading to fragmentation and the rise of local rulers. After Tauke's death in 1715/1718, the khanate lost unity, and the three hordes became separate khanates. During the 17th century, the Kazakhs fought the Oirats. The early 18th century marked the height of the khanate. The Little Horde participated in the 1723–1730 war against the Dzungar Khanate, following the "Great Disaster," achieving notable victories at the Bulanty River in 1726 and at Añyraqai in 1729. Ablai Khan played a major role in the wars against the Dzungars during the 1720s–1750s, earning the title of "batyr" ("hero"), and ruled the Middle Zhuz from 1771 to 1781. In 1740, Ablai accepted Russian suzerainty while maintaining a policy of balancing between the Russian Empire and the Qing dynasty, allowing the khanate to retain autonomy. After his death, his son Vali Khan (1781–1819) abandoned independence and acknowledged Russian suzerainty. In 1822, the khanate institution among the Kazakh hordes was formally abolished, leading to the uprising of Sultan Qasym in 1824–1827. The last serious effort to revive the khanate was led by Sultan Kenesary Qasymov, who in 1837 proclaimed himself khan and conducted an armed struggle against Russian authorities until his death in 1847. Following incorporation into the Russian Empire, Kazakh intellectuals led a cultural renaissance more advanced than that of other Central Asian peoples. Figures like Shoqan Walikhanov and Abay Kunanbayev adapted modern ideas to create a secular, dynamic Kazakh culture, distinguishing them from other Central Asian movements. Despite their nomadic lifestyle, the Kazakhs were one of the most literate and progressive indigenous groups in the region. In the wake of the Russian Revolution, the Alash Orda government was formed in 1917 as an attempt to secure Kazakh autonomy, though it existed only in name. It played a significant role in promoting modern Kazakh education, culture, and national consciousness. The Bolshevik Red Army defeated White Russian forces by 1920, and Kazakhstan was incorporated into the Soviet Union. Despite their nomadic lifestyle, the Kazakhs were one of the most literate indigenous groups in Central Asia. However, Soviet forced collectivization devastated the population, with a 20% drop between 1926 and 1939, resulting in 1.5 million deaths primarily due to starvation and related diseases, and some from violence. Thousands fled to China, though most did not survive. Kazakhstan became a full Soviet republic in 1936. The Virgin Lands Program, launched in the 1950s, opened northern Kazakhstan to wheat farming by Slavic settlers, causing an ecological disaster that severely impacted the Aral Sea. During the Soviet period, Kazakhstan’s strategic importance grew with the establishment of a space-launch center and nuclear testing sites. From 1959 to 1986, Dinmukhamed Kunayev, the first secretary of the Communist Party of Kazakhstan, dominated regional politics, balancing the interests of Kazakhs and Russians. However, his removal by Mikhail Gorbachev in 1986 led to the Jeltoqsan riots, the first serious protests in the Soviet Union during the 1980s, signaling widespread discontent. Kazakhstan declared sovereignty on 25 October 1990 and became fully independent on 16 December 1991, after the collapse of the Soviet Union. Humans have inhabited Kazakhstan since the Lower Paleolithic, generally pursuing nomadic pastoralism suitable for the region’s climate and terrain. Prehistoric Bronze Age cultures such as the Srubna, Afanasevo, and Andronovo extended into the region. Between 500 BC and 500 AD, Kazakhstan was home to the Saka and the Huns, early nomadic warrior cultures. According to the Journal of Archaeological Science, in July 2020, scientists from South Ural State University studied two Late Bronze Age horses from Kurgan 5 of the Novoilinovsky 2 cemetery in the Kostanay region using radiocarbon dating. Researcher Igor Chechushkov indicated that the Andronovites were riding horses several centuries earlier than previously assumed. The stallion was nearly 20 years old and the mare was 18 years old. Animals were buried with the person they accompanied throughout their lives and were used for food, harnessing vehicles, and riding. At the beginning of the first millennium, the steppes east of the Caspian were inhabited by nomads speaking Indo-European and Uralic languages, including the Alans, Aorsi, Budini, Issedones/Wusun, Madjars, Massagetae, and Sakas. Their names, relations, and compositions were sometimes fluid and interchangeable. Some formed states, such as Yancai (northwest of the Aral Sea) and Kangju in the east. Over centuries, Turkic and other exogenous languages dominated the region, arriving with nomadic invaders and settlers from the east. Following the Huns’ entry, many previous inhabitants migrated westward into Europe or were absorbed by the Huns. The Hun Empire gradually shifted westward into Eastern Europe. Events in future Kazakhstan are unclear and often based on mythic or apocryphal folk tales from peoples who migrated westward. From the middle of the 2nd century, the Yueban—an offshoot of the Xiongnu and possibly connected to the Huns—established a state in far-eastern Kazakhstan. Over the next few centuries, peoples such as the Akatziri, Avars (known later as the Pannonian Avars), Sabirs, and Bulgars migrated through the area and into the Caucasus and Eastern Europe. By the beginning of the 6th century, the proto-Mongolian Rouran Khaganate annexed areas that later became part of eastern Kazakhstan. The Göktürks, formerly subject to the Rouran, migrated westward, pushing the Huns west and south. By the mid-6th century, the First Turkic Khaganate was established. A civil war led to its split into the Eastern and Western Turkic Khaganates. In 630 and 659, these were invaded and conquered by Tang China. Toward the end of the 7th century, the two states were reunited in the Second Turkic Khaganate, which began to fragment a few generations later. In 766, the Oghuz Yabgu State (Oguz il) was founded with its capital in Jankent and occupied most of later Kazakhstan. It was established by the Oghuz Turks, refugees from the Turgesh Kaganate. The Oghuz lost a struggle with the Karluks for control of Turgesh, and other Oghuz clans migrated from Turgesh-controlled Zhetysu to the Karatau Mountains and the Chu valley in the Issyk Kul basin. In the eighth and ninth centuries, portions of southern Kazakhstan were conquered by Arabs who introduced Islam. The Oghuz Turks controlled western Kazakhstan from the ninth through the 11th centuries, while Turkic peoples of the Kipchaks and Kimaks controlled the east at the same time. The Cumans controlled western Kazakhstan from around the 12th century until the 1220s. These vast lands became known as Dashti-Kipchak or the Kipchak Steppe. During the ninth century, the Qarluq confederation formed the Qarakhanid state, which conquered Transoxiana (the area north and east of the Oxus River, present-day Amu Darya). Beginning in the early 11th century, the Qarakhanids fought among themselves and with the Seljuk Turks to the south. The Qarakhanids, who converted to Islam, were conquered in the 1130s by the Kara-Khitan (moved west from North China). In the mid-12th century, an independent state of Khorazm along the Oxus River broke away from the weakening Karakitai, but the bulk of the Kara-Khitan lasted until the Mongol invasion of Genghis Khan from 1219 to 1221. During Mongol advancement into Desht-i-Kipchak lands, some Cuman-Kipchak leaders fought the Mongols, but most joined them and became part of the Mongol Empire’s military force, led by Batu Khan, who began conquering Eastern Europe in 1237. According to one version, it was due to these tribes that the mixed term "Tatar-Mongols" emerged. In the latter 13th century, the western part of the empire, ruled by Jochi (the eldest son of Genghis Khan), broke away and established the independent Golden Horde. All later rulers of it came from the Jochi lineage. During Uzbeg Khan’s rule (1312–1341), Islam was adopted as a state religion. According to the latest population genetics research, mainly of autosomal markers and Y-chromosome polymorphism, the Kazakh ethnicity emerged during the 13th to 15th centuries. After the dissolution of the Golden Horde, the Uzbek Khanate was formed on most of modern Kazakhstan’s territory. Under Abu'l-Khayr Khan, the country was weak and the government corrupt. Two children of Barak Khan, Janibek and Kerei Khan, gathered Kazakh people to Jetysu, where they founded the Independent Kazakh Khanate. Shoqan Walikhanov believed that the reasons Kazakhs created large tribal unions to form the Kazakh Khanate were to retain their nomadic territories and secure their rights in lands where they migrated. In 1500, the Uzbeks concluded peace with the Kazakhs, and the Kazakh Khanate gained sovereignty from Shaybanid control. All former Uzbek Khanate lands north of the Syr Darya were transferred to the Kazakh Khanate. In 1499, Muhammad Shaybani, the grandson of Abu'l-Khayr, was forced to march south with loyal steppe tribes into Mawarannahr. There, he conquered the fragmented Timurid state, which had collapsed after Timur’s death. He moved the capital from Sygnak to Bukhara, where in 1500 he established the Bukhara Khanate. The nomadic Desht-Kipchak tribes that joined Shaybani mixed with the local sedentary population—the Turkic-speaking Sarts, the ancient Turkic Karluks, and, as victors, gave their new people the name Uzbeks. In the early 16th century, the Kazakhs transformed the khanate into a nomadic empire stretching across the steppes east of the Caspian Sea and north of the Aral Sea as far as the upper Irtysh River and the western approaches to the Altai Mountains. Shaybani marched south with the remaining loyal Steppe tribes into Mawarannahr, where he conquered the fragmented Timurid state that had collapsed after Timur’s death. He moved the capital from Sygnak to Bukhara, establishing a new state there in 1500—the Bukhara Khanate. The nomadic Desht-Kipchak tribes that joined Shaybani intermingled with the local sedentary populations, including the Turkic-speaking Sarts and the ancient Karluks, and adopted the name Uzbeks. In the early 16th century, the Kazakhs transformed the Khanate into a nomadic empire stretching across the steppes east of the Caspian Sea and north of the Aral Sea, reaching as far as the upper Irtysh River and the western approaches to the Altai Mountains. During the reigns of Burunduk Khan (1488–1509) and Kasym Khan (1509–18), the Kazakhs dominated the entire steppe region, reportedly fielding 200,000 cavalry and being feared by neighbors. Many historians consider Kasym Khan’s leadership the beginning of a distinct and sovereign Kazakh state, extending Kazakh authority from southeastern modern Kazakhstan to the Ural Mountains. Mirza Muhammad Haidar Dughlat wrote in his Tarikh-i-Rashidi that Kasym Khan became the absolute ruler over all of Dasht-i-Kipchak, with an army numbering over a million men, gaining fame and power unmatched since Juji Khan. During Kasym Khan’s reign (1511–1523), the Khanate expanded through numerous victories, gaining recognition even in Western Europe, and the first Kazakh code of laws, Qasym Khannyn Qasqa Zholy (Bright Road of Kasym Khan), was established in 1520. Between 1522 and 1538, the Khanate experienced its first civil war. Historical texts such as Tarikh-i-Rashidi (1541–1545) by Muhammad Haidar Dughlat and Zhamigi-at-Tavarikh (1598–1599) by Kadyrgali Kosynuli Zhalayir describe the Khanate. During the reign of Kasym Khan’s three sons, khan authority weakened, leading to the fragmentation of the Khanate into three hordes: the Great Horde in southeastern Kazakhstan north of the Tien Shan, the Middle Horde in the central steppe near the Aral Sea, and the Little Horde between the Aral Sea and the Ural River. In these regions, the khan’s power was constrained by tribal leaders known as sultans and clan heads such as beys and batyrs. Haqnazar Khan, the final son of Kasym Khan to rule, reunified the fractured hordes and led aggressive military campaigns, including systematic raids into Transoxania, with Tauekel Khan temporarily capturing Samarkand. His influence extended to the Bashkirs, Kyrgyzes, and Nogais, and included the Khanates of Kazan, Sibir, and Astrakhan, as well as cities like Bukhara, Khiva, and Tashkent. Tauekel Khan’s rule saw Tashkent become part of the Khanate in 1598, later serving as its capital. Tole Bi Alibekuly (1663–1756), a statesman from the Dulat tribe of the Senior Zhuz, ruled Tashkent and oversaw the construction of many architectural structures now recognized as historical landmarks; he was buried in Tashkent, and his mausoleum remains a key attraction. After Tauekel’s death in 1715/1718, the Khanate lost unity, and the three hordes became separate khanates. In 1643, the Kazakh-Dzungar wars erupted, dividing the population into three tribes called juzes: senior, middle, and junior. During the reign of Ablai Khan (1771–1781), all Kazakhs were united to fight the Dzungars. Ablai participated in major battles against the Dzungars from the 1720s to the 1750s, earning the title of "batyr" ("hero"), and became the last khan whose authority was recognized across the steppe, ruling the Middle Zhuz. In 1740, Ablai accepted Russian suzerainty while balancing between the Russian Empire and the Qing dynasty, preserving relative autonomy. After his death, his son Vali Khan (1781–1819) abandoned independence and acknowledged Russian authority. In 1822, the Khanate institution was abolished, sparking the uprising of Sultan Qasym (1824–1827). The final attempt to restore the Khanate was led by Sultan Kenesary Qasymov, who proclaimed himself khan in 1837 and fought Russian authorities until his death in 1847. Russian traders and soldiers began appearing on the northwestern edge of Kazakh territory in the 17th century, when Cossacks established forts that became Yaitsk (modern Oral) and Guryev (modern Atyrau). The Russians seized Kazakh territory because the khanates were preoccupied with the Zunghar Oirats, who moved into the region from the east in the late 16th century, forcing the Kazakhs westward and placing them between the Kalmyks and Russians. In the first half of the 1700s, conflicts with the Dzungars surged; in 1730, Abul Khayr, a khan of the Lesser Horde, sought Russian assistance, though his intent was a temporary alliance against the Kalmyks, and the Russians gained control of the Lesser Horde. They conquered the Middle Horde by 1798, while the Great Horde remained independent until the 1820s, when the expanding Kokand khanate forced its khans to accept Russian protection. The Russian Empire began integrating the Kazakh steppe; between 1822 and 1848, the three main khans of the Lesser, Middle, and Great Hordes were suspended. Russians built many forts and provided land to settlers, while nomadic tribes received less grazing land, leading to sedentary lifestyles. Between 5 and 15 percent of the Kazakh Steppe population were immigrants due to Russian policy. Nineteenth-century colonization was slowed by rebellions such as those led by Isatay Taymanuly and Makhambet Utemisuly (1836–1838) and Eset Kotibaruli (1847–1858). In 1863, the Russian Empire announced a policy to annex troublesome border areas, leading to the conquest of most of Central Asia and the creation of two administrative districts: the General-Gubernatorstvo of Russian Turkestan and the Steppes, with most of present-day Kazakhstan, including Almaty (Verny), in the latter. During the 19th century, Kazakhs had a high numeracy level, rising from about 72% in 1820 to about 88% in 1880, surpassing Russians at the time. This early numeracy may be attributed to a small settler share, good nutritional conditions, and contact learning from Russian settlers in the 1870s and 1880s, which encouraged Kazakhs to invest in education. In the early 19th century, Russian forts limited the grazing areas of nomadic tribes, and the final disruption of nomadism began in the 1890s with the introduction of Russian settlers into fertile northern and eastern Kazakhstan. In 1906, the Trans-Aral Railway between Orenburg and Tashkent was completed, facilitating Russian colonization of Zhetysu. Between 1906 and 1912, over half a million Russian farms were established under reforms by Russian Minister of the Interior Petr Stolypin, pressuring traditional Kazakh life by occupying grazing land and using scarce water. Vasile Balabanov, the administrator for Turkestan, oversaw this resettlement. Starving and displaced, many Kazakhs joined the Basmachi movement in resistance to conscription ordered by the tsar in July 1916 during World War I. Russian forces suppressed the resistance, killing thousands and forcing many to flee to China and Mongolia. Many Kazakhs and Russians resisted the Communist takeover until 1920. In the second half of the 20th century, Russia built schools in Kazakhstan, forming an elite class. Most educated Kazakhs belonged to the Constitutional Democratic Party, which later fractured, leading to the formation of the Alash party, named after a legendary founder of the Kazakh people. Alash aimed to establish an independent democratic Kazakh state and formed the Alash Orda, which lasted until 1920 when the Bolsheviks banned it. The Alash Orda covered most of modern Kazakhstan, excluding southern regions. The Turkestan Orda or Kokand Autonomy was an unrecognized state formed on 27 November 1917 and existing until 22 February 1918; it was a secular republic headed by a president. The Kirghiz Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic was established in 1920 and renamed the Kazakh Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic in 1925 when the Kazakhs were officially distinguished from the Kyrgyz by the Soviet government. The Russian Empire had recognized the ethnic difference but used the term "Kirghiz" to avoid confusion with Cossacks. In 1925, the original capital Orenburg was reincorporated into Russian territory, and Kyzylorda became the capital until 1929. Almaty (Alma-Ata during the Soviet period) became the new capital in 1929. In 1936, the territory was officially separated from the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic (RSFSR) and became the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, the second-largest republic in the Soviet Union, with an area of 2,717,300 km² (1,049,200 sq mi). The first Kazakh famine began in 1919 during the Russian Civil War, when livestock dropped from 30 million to 16 million, leaving nearly a million people starving, and factories ceased operations. From 1929 to 1934, during Stalin’s collectivization campaign, Kazakhstan endured repeated famines known as Asharshylyk, similar to the Holodomor in Ukraine, with over one million residents and 80 percent of the livestock dying. Thousands attempted to escape to China, but most starved. Robert Conquest stated that the Soviet policy imposed an untried stereotype on a functioning social order, resulting in disproportionate death and suffering. During the 1930s, the Soviet government built Gulags across the Union, with 11 concentration camps in Kazakhstan, the most well-known being ALZhIR. NKVD Order 00486 of 15 August 1937 initiated mass repression against ChSIR (members of families of traitors to the Motherland), allowing arrests without evidence and sending women to camps for the first time. In a few months, over 18,000 women were arrested, and about 8,000 served time in ALZhIR—the Akmolinsk Camp of Wives of Traitors to the Motherland. These included wives of statesmen, politicians, and former Alash members. After the camps closed in 1953, it was reported that 1,507 women gave birth as a result of being raped by guards. Most former Alash members worked on translating textbooks for newly established schools, as most Kazakhs were still uneducated. Some joined the Communist Party, but the elite continued to protest Soviet policies, especially collectivization, which caused the 1930–33 famine. The Soviet government attempted to suppress and imprison Kazakh elites, and due to harsh conditions in the Kazakh gulags, imprisoned former Alash members experienced accelerated aging. Through the lens of the front lines and home front, Roberto Carmack argues that World War II intensified Kazakhstan’s integration into the Soviet Union, while also worsening ethnic tensions and social disparities. The war reinforced ethnic chauvinism and solidified Russia’s dominance in the USSR, despite Sovietizing the Kazakh populace through propaganda, military service, and exposure to other parts of the Union. A total of 1.2 million soldiers from Kazakhstan were mobilized, in addition to 178,000 already serving in the Soviet military. Kazakh soldiers participated in all major battles of World War II, including hundreds among the defenders of the Brest Fortress at the beginning of the war. During the Battle of Moscow, which began in late September 1941, the 316th Rifle Division included Kazakh soldiers.

World War II significantly deepened Kazakhstan’s integration into the Soviet Union, as argued by Roberto Carmack, through both frontline military involvement and domestic propaganda efforts. The war intensified ethnic tensions and social inequalities, with ethnic chauvinism sometimes overriding national security concerns. Soviet propaganda, combined with military service and exposure to other parts of the USSR, led to the Sovietization of the Kazakh population and the Kazakh SSR. Approximately 1.2 million Kazakh soldiers were conscripted, in addition to 178,000 already serving, and participated in all major battles, including the defense of the Brest Fortress at the war’s outset. During the Battle of Moscow in late 1941, the 316th and 312th Rifle Divisions, under Generals I.V. Panfilov and Colonel A.F. Naumov, performed notably, while the 1073rd Rifle Regiment, led by Bauyrzhan Momyshuly, showed heroic resistance. Political officers such as P.B. Vikhrev, M. Gabdullin, and machine gunner T. Tokhtarov also displayed exceptional bravery. From 6 September 1941, Kazakh units actively defended Leningrad, entered the Stalingrad front in summer 1942, and fought in the Battle of Kursk, ultimately liberating Belarus, the Baltics, Moldova, Ukraine, and Eastern European countries. The 47th Separate Guards Tank Brigade, commanded by Galya Adilbekovich Adilbekov, fought heroically in the Battle of the Dnieper and the liberation of Kyiv, and had previously proven himself in the Battle of Vitebsk (1941), the counteroffensive near Trubchevsk (1941), and the Battle of Stalingrad (1942). Adilbekov was the only Central Asian national to hold the rank of Guard Lieutenant Colonel and commanded a separate Guards Tank Regiment at the time of his death. Hundreds of thousands of Kazakh soldiers were awarded Soviet honors, including 96,638 Kazakhs, and 497 individuals—among them 98 Kazakhs—received the title of Hero of the Soviet Union, including women like machine gunner M. Mametova and sniper A. Moldagulova, and pilots T.Y. Begeldinov, L.I. Beda, I.F. Pavlov, and S.D. Lugansky, each honored twice. During the war, many citizens from western USSR regions and industrial centers were relocated to the Kazakh SSR, including Crimean Tatars, Germans, North Caucasus Muslims, and Poles from eastern Poland, with local people sharing food with the newcomers. Between 1953 and 1965, during Khrushchev’s Virgin Lands Campaign (1958–1964), large areas of grazing land were cultivated for wheat and cereals, and further settlement occurred in the late 1960s and 1970s when the Soviet government offered bonuses to relocate industry to Central Asia’s coal, gas, and oil regions. By the 1970s, the Kazakh SSR became the only Soviet republic where Russians outnumbered Kazakhs due to immigration and the decline of the nomadic population. The republic played key industrial and agricultural roles in the Soviet economy, with coal deposits promising to replace depleted European fuel reserves, though the distance between European centers and the coal fields created logistical challenges. This left a mixed legacy after 1991: a population nearly equal in size between Russians and Kazakhs, a class of Russian technocrats essential to economic development but ethnically distinct, and a coal- and oil-based energy sector hampered by poor infrastructure. On 16 December 1986, the Soviet Politburo dismissed Dinmukhamed Konayev, the long-serving Communist Party leader of Kazakhstan, and appointed non-Kazakh Gennady Kolbin from Ulyanovsk, triggering protests that resulted in between two and twenty deaths, 763 and 1137 injuries, and between 2,212 and 2,336 arrests. Kolbin’s plans to purge the Communist Youth League were blocked by Moscow, and in September 1989 he was replaced by Kazakh Nursultan Nazarbayev. In June 1990, Moscow declared central sovereignty over Kazakhstan, forcing the republic to issue its own sovereignty statement, which heightened tensions between the numerically equal Kazakh and Russian communities. Demonstrations by both groups around the parliament building in August sought to influence the final statement, adopted in October. Parliament named Nazarbayev chairman and converted the role to president. Unlike other republic leaders, especially Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, Nazarbayev remained loyal to the Soviet Union in 1991 because he believed economic interdependence made independence unviable. However, he sought to control Kazakhstan’s mineral wealth and industrial potential. This became critical after 1990 when Gorbachev negotiated with American Chevron to develop the Tengiz oil field without consulting Nazarbayev; at his insistence, Moscow relinquished control of Kazakhstan’s mineral resources in June 1991, and Gorbachev’s authority collapsed. Nazarbayev supported Gorbachev and a union structure, urging other republic leaders to sign a treaty forming the Union of Sovereign States, which Gorbachev had drafted as a final effort to preserve the USSR. The treaty was never implemented due to the August 1991 coup attempt against Gorbachev. Nazarbayev did not condemn the coup until its second day but continued to support Gorbachev and a union due to his belief that independence would be economically disastrous. During this time, Nazarbayev began preparing Kazakhstan for greater autonomy or independence, appointing professional economists and managers and seeking foreign expertise. The outlawing of the Communist Party of Kazakhstan after the coup allowed Nazarbayev to take near-total control of the economy, which had been under Soviet management until late 1991. He secured his position by winning an uncontested presidential election in December 1991. A week after the election, he became president of an independent Kazakhstan when Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus signed documents dissolving the Soviet Union. He convened a meeting of the leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan, proposing a Turkic confederation as a counterweight to the Slavic states, which convinced the Slavic leaders to include Kazakhstan in a revised dissolution document. The capital’s name was used for the Alma-Ata Protocol, the foundational declaration of the Commonwealth of Independent States. Post-Soviet countries have since signed multilateral and bilateral treaties to resolve the Soviet Union’s legacy. On 16 December 1991, five days before the formal declaration, Kazakhstan became the last republic to proclaim independence. The republic followed the same political pattern as the other Central Asian states, retaining its government structure and leadership from 1990 onward. Nazarbayev, elected president in 1991, remained in undisputed power through 1995. He ensured his position by making the prime minister and Council of Ministers directly accountable to the president in the 1993 constitution and reinforcing that structure in a 1995 revision. Opposition parties were legally restricted, and Nazarbayev gained popularity by minimizing the economic shock of independence and maintaining ethnic harmony in a country with over 100 nationalities. In December 1994, Nazarbayev signed the Budapest Memorandum with Russia, the United Kingdom, and the United States, denuclearizing Kazakhstan, with Ukraine and Belarus signing similar agreements in a joint ceremony at the Budapest Convention Center. In 1997, the capital was moved from Almaty to Astana, and homosexuality was decriminalized the following year. In March 2019, President Nazarbayev resigned after 29 years in office but retained influence through the Security Council and held the formal title Leader of the Nation. Kassym-Jomart Tokayev succeeded him as president, and his first act was to rename the capital from Astana to Nur-Sultan after Nazarbayev. In June 2019, Tokayev won the presidential election. In January 2022, Tokayev took over the powerful Security Council, removing Nazarbayev from the post following violent protests over fuel prices. Tokayev later proposed constitutional amendments to limit his own power and remove Nazarbayev’s formal title as Leader of the Nation. The amendments were approved in a 2022 referendum. In September 2022, the capital’s name was changed back to Astana from Nur-Sultan. During the 1990s, although Russia remained the primary economic and security partner, Nazarbayev promoted ties with China, the Central Asian nations, and the West. However, Kazakhstan remains primarily dependent on Russia. The Baikonur Cosmodrome, built in the 1950s for the Soviet space program, is located near Tyuratam and the city of Baikonur. Kazakhstan maintains strong relations with the United States, being the 78th-largest trading partner with $2.5 billion in two-way trade and the first country to recognize it after independence. In 1994 and 1995, the U.S. assisted Kazakhstan in eliminating all nuclear warheads after it abandoned its nuclear program and closed the Semipalatinsk Test Sites, with the last sites and tunnels shut down by 1995. In 2010, U.S. President Barack Obama met with Nazarbayev at the Nuclear Security Summit in Washington, DC, to strengthen strategic ties, enhance nuclear safety, and promote regional stability and economic growth.
